task1.title: Task 1 (20 minutes, at least 150 words)
task1.prompt:
The table below shows the percentage of households with access to the internet in four countries in 2000, 2010, and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

| Country | 2000 | 2010 | 2020 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Country A | 5% | 45% | 92% |
| Country B | 2% | 20% | 68% |
| Country C | 15% | 60% | 95% |
| Country D | 1% | 10% | 40% |
task1.sample_band6:
The table shows how many households had internet access in four countries over a 20 year period, from 2000 to 2020.

In 2000, all four countries had low internet access, with Country C the highest at 15% and Country D the lowest at only 1%. Country A and Country B also started low, at 5% and 2%.

By 2010, access had grown a lot in every country. Country C was still the highest with 60%, and Country A grew to 45%. Country B reached 20%, while Country D only grew to 10%, which was much slower than the others.

By 2020, Country C and Country A had the highest access, at 95% and 92%. Country B also grew a lot to 68%. Country D grew too but stayed behind the rest at 40%, less than half of Country C.

Overall, all countries increased internet access a lot, but Country D grew much more slowly than the other three countries, especially Country A and Country C, which ended up close to full access.
task1.sample_band8:
The table illustrates the proportion of households with internet access in four countries at three points between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, internet access rose dramatically in all four countries over the period, although Country D consistently lagged well behind the other three, which converged on broadly similar, near-universal levels by 2020.

In 2000, access was minimal everywhere, ranging from a mere 1% in Country D to 15% in Country C, which held a clear early lead. Over the following decade, uptake accelerated sharply: by 2010, Country C had reached 60% and Country A had climbed to 45%, while Country B's figure stood at 20%. Country D, by contrast, had crept up to only 10%, barely a tenth of Country C's rate at that time.

By 2020, this pattern of divergence had narrowed considerably for three of the four countries. Country C and Country A had both reached levels above 90%, at 95% and 92% respectively, with Country B not far behind at 68%. Country D, however, had reached just 40%, meaning that despite a fourfold increase since 2000, it remained well under half the rate recorded in the three leading countries. This gap suggests that whatever factors drove rapid adoption elsewhere were considerably weaker, or slower to take hold, in Country D.

task2.title: Task 2 (40 minutes, at least 250 words)
task2.prompt:
Some people believe that technology has made our lives more complicated, while others think it has made life easier.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
task2.sample_band6:
Technology is a big part of modern life, and people have different opinions about whether it makes life easier or more complicated. In this essay, I will discuss both views and then give my own opinion.

On one hand, many people think technology makes life more complicated. For example, we now have to remember many passwords, learn how to use new apps, and deal with problems like slow internet or broken devices. Also, some older people find new technology confusing and stressful, because it changes so fast and they cannot keep up with every update.

On the other hand, other people believe technology has made life much easier. For instance, we can now pay bills online instead of waiting in long lines, we can talk to family members in other countries for free using video calls, and we can find information instantly instead of going to a library. These things save a lot of time and effort compared to the past.

In my opinion, technology has made life easier overall, even though it does create some new problems. The time it saves on daily tasks like shopping, banking, and communication is much bigger than the small difficulties of learning new systems. I believe most people would not want to go back to life without modern technology, which shows that its benefits are generally seen as greater than its drawbacks.

In conclusion, while technology can be complicated at times, I think it has mostly made modern life more convenient and efficient.
task2.sample_band8:
Technology's impact on daily life is a frequent subject of debate, with some arguing it has introduced unnecessary complexity, while others maintain it has simplified life considerably. This essay will examine both perspectives before outlining my own view.

Those who see technology as a complicating force often point to the sheer volume of devices, accounts, and updates a typical person must now manage. Remembering dozens of passwords, troubleshooting malfunctioning software, and adapting to constantly changing interfaces can be genuinely draining, particularly for older adults or those with limited technical confidence. There is also a subtler cost: the expectation of constant availability, created by smartphones and messaging apps, can blur the boundary between work and personal time in ways earlier generations never had to negotiate.

Equally compelling, however, is the case that technology has removed far greater burdens than it has created. Tasks that once consumed hours — paying bills, researching information, or communicating with relatives abroad — can now be completed in moments, often from a single device. Medical diagnoses, educational resources, and professional opportunities that were once restricted by geography or cost are increasingly accessible to anyone with an internet connection, representing a genuine levelling of opportunity rather than a mere convenience.

In my view, the complications technology introduces are real but ultimately secondary to the efficiency it delivers. Most of the frustrations associated with technology, such as learning a new interface, are temporary and one-off, whereas the time saved through digital tools compounds daily, over years. Consequently, I would argue that technology has, on balance, simplified life far more than it has complicated it, even if that simplification occasionally comes with a short-term learning cost.

In conclusion, while technology undeniably creates new demands on our attention and patience, its overall effect has been to make everyday life considerably more efficient and accessible than it was in the past.
